transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-05
Start: 15:00 EST
Duration: ~41 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Northpoint CTO), Robert Li (Northpoint CISO), Jason Greene (Head of Ops)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Northpoint's data residency and compliance constraints for evaluating Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Main concerns: EU data residency for retail business, strict logging retention and redaction rules for financial transactions, SOC2/HIPAA overlap for specific products, KMS/BYOK and HSM requirements, and procurement timeline. Next steps agreed: share compliance artifacts, architecture diagram, and schedule deep dive.

Topics:
- Data residency (EU, US regional separation)
- Logging & audit log retention + masking/pseudonymization
- Encryption, KMS / BYOK, HSM requirements
- Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs (latency/cost/control)
- Subprocessor list and legal controls (DPAs)
- Timeline for procurement / pilot

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, I'm Alex Moreno from Redwood, I'm the AE on this account, with me is Priya Shah, our solutions engineer. Um, thanks for making time.
[00:07] Maya: Hey Alex, thanks, hi Priya, quick note we have about 40 minutes, so want to focus on residency and the things our compliance team flagged.
[00:12] Priya: Great, Maya. Could you, uh, kick off with high-level constraints so we can map to Hosted/Dedicated/Private?
[00:18] Maya: Sure. So Northpoint's consumer banking product has EU customers; legally we need transactional data for EU customers to stay in the EU — ideally within a region we control. We also have a set of payments product flows that may fall under PSD2 and some HR data that touches HIPAA-ish controls for employee health info. The compliance team wants to know what logs Redwood keeps, for how long, and whether we can turn off storing PII or mask it server-side.
[00:38] Robert: And to add, our security folks need to see KMS options — BYOK is a hard requirement for Dedicated/Private, and for hosted we need to know if there's a customer-managed key option or HSM integration. Also, audit logs, tamper-evidence, and retention windows — we can't ship logs out for more than 7 years for certain records, and some logs need redaction.
[00:56] Alex: Understood. At a high level, Redwood Hosted keeps metadata and request logs in our control plane but we do have options. For customers with strict residency needs we recommend Redwood Dedicated or Redwood Private, where the control plane can be placed inside the customer's VPC or on-prem. Priya will walk through the specifics.
[01:12] Priya: Yep. So quick bucket: Hosted API (fastest), Dedicated (reserved capacity on our infra, can be isolated to a region and provide stronger data isolation), and Private (we ship a private control plane into your VPC or on-premises). For EU-only residency we normally do Dedicated pinned to an EU region or Private deployed into their EU VPC.
[01:34] Jason: Is Dedicated actually in our tenancy or is it like a shared pool? We need to understand the isolation model.
[01:40] Priya: Good question. Dedicated is dedicated GPU pools for your account — compute is isolated to your provisioned capacity, tenant metadata may still be in Redwood's control plane unless you opt for Private where the control plane runs in your VPC. There's sometimes confusion around that — we can provide a diagram.
[01:54] Maya: That distinction is important. If the control plane is outside our network the legal folks push back on some categories of logs being exported.
[02:01] Alex: Totally. For sensitive flows we often recommend Private so the control plane and audit logs never leave your network and you can enforce egress rules. If Private isn't feasible, Dedicated plus strict contractual DPAs and subprocessor commitments is the middle ground.
[02:12] Robert: About log content — do you capture full request bodies? Specifically, do you persist prompt text, completions, or tokens in logs?
[02:20] Priya: Out of box Hosted will persist request and response payloads for a short retention for debugging and analytics; we offer configurable retention and can disable payload persistence for Dedicated/Private. There's also a feature to strip or hash PII server-side before logs are written. Some customers send tokens to our staging telemetry but we can configure that to be opt-out.
[02:40] Robert: Can you do server-side redaction for account numbers and names, like regex-based or tokenization?
[02:44] Priya: Yes, we support regex-based scrubbing and a pseudonymization module. For Private deployments you can run your own scrubbing pipeline before logs are captured so nothing sensitive ever hits Redwood logs.
[02:55] Maya: For GDPR we need a process for data deletion and proof of deletion — e.g. if a user requests erasure, how quickly can you purge logs and model caches? Also, are KV caches considered persistent storage?
[03:07] Priya: Good point. KV cache — sometimes folks call it KV cash in notes, sorry — is used for inference speed. For Hosted it's a managed cache; we have TTL controls and we can flush caches on a per-tenant basis. For Dedicated/Private you get control to purge caches programmatically. Deletion requests: we provide APIs to delete stored artifacts and a retention policy; we can also generate deletion certificates for audits.
[03:28] Robert: Certificates would be helpful. Also chain of custody requirements — we need audit logs with tamper-evidence and time-synced entries.
[03:34] Priya: Our audit logs include immutability flags and are append-only. For Private, customers can forward logs to their SIEM directly, and you can retain them under your own retention policy. For Hosted, we maintain logs for a configurable default but will honor contractual obligations for longer retention when agreed.
[03:50] Jason: Network controls — can you restrict egress from the model to specific IPs and prevent data exfil to third-party sub-processors?
[03:57] Alex: Yes, for Private we put the control plane inside your VPC so egress is managed by your network ACLs; Dedicated can be configured with VPC peering and strict egress rules. We also publish a subprocessor list and can negotiate constraints in the DPA.
[04:10] Maya: On keys — BYOK is required for anything with EU PII. Is there a HSM-backed KMS option in Hosted?
[04:15] Priya: For Hosted we have a customer-managed key flow where keys are stored in major cloud KMS providers — you can bring keys via your cloud KMS (BYOK), and for higher assurance we support HSM-backed keys in Dedicated/Private. For Hosted we currently integrate with AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and Azure Key Vault.
[04:33] Robert: What about sub-processor transparency? We want to avoid surprises — if you deploy an open-source model that pulls in a related hosting provider, we need to know.
[04:41] Alex: We'll share the subprocessor list — it's part of our compliance pack. We also document where models run and what kernels/hardware are used. For customers with strict controls we recommend Private so you can manage the model artifacts entirely.
[04:54] Maya: Any differences in SLAs or latency expectations between Dedicated and Private? We're sensitive to 200–300ms p50 for autocomplete flows.
[05:02] Priya: Dedicated is designed for predictable throughput with SLA-backed capacity and can meet low latency with provisioned units. Private latency depends on your on-prem infra — if you provision equivalent GPU resources, latency is similar. Hosting region choice also matters for EU vs US. We can run benchmarks with your sample prompts to validate p50/p95.
[05:20] Jason: Are there limits on what you can or cannot log for financial transactions? Some of our logs include masked PANs, some include cleartext for reconciliation — need to make sure masked fields stay masked.
[05:29] Priya: Masking policies are configurable. We can enforce masking at the ingestion layer, and for Private you can run custom scrubbing before ingestion. For Hosted, we offer masking rules and will sign contractual clauses around never exporting unmasked PANs for EU customers.
[05:43] Robert: Regarding HIPAA, some of our HR flows may be considered PHI. Do you have a BAA or approach for handling HIPAA-covered data?
[05:51] Alex: Redwood can sign a BAA for covered use cases. We treat HIPAA as a class of compliance that requires dedicated controls: encryption at rest/in transit (always), restricted access, and auditability. For any PHI flows we typically recommend Dedicated or Private and a signed BAA.
[06:07] Maya: Procurement timeline — we're trying to run a pilot in Q2 and procurement complete by end of Q2. What kind of lead times for Dedicated/Private?
[06:16] Alex: Dedicated setup can be done in 2–4 weeks once contract is signed; Private depends on on-prem or VPC configuration, usually 4–8 weeks. We can get a minimal Dedicated pilot faster.
[06:27] Jason: Cost tradeoffs — how much more is Dedicated vs Hosted? High level ballpark is fine.
[06:31] Priya: Hosted is usage-based and typically lower for early-stage usage. Dedicated has a monthly committed capacity cost plus usage; Dedicated can be ~2–4x more depending on throughput needs. Private includes additional engineering/setup fees. We'll share a pricing sheet.
[06:43] Robert: Another question: model fine-tuning and storing fine-tuned weights — do you keep a copy? Is that considered customer data?
[06:50] Priya: Fine-tuned artifacts are treated as customer-owned assets. For Hosted we store them encrypted, and access is restricted; for Private you can store them in your infrastructure. We can also support ephemeral fine-tuning where artifacts are available only for a defined retention window.
[07:04] Maya: Are you already SOC2 Type II? Any ISO certs?
[07:08] Alex: Yes, Redwood is SOC2 Type II and we have ISO27001. We'll send the reports; they're part of what we'll share after the call.
[07:16] Maya: Great. On data subject requests for EU customers, we need an API or process for search and erasure across logs and model artifacts.
[07:23] Priya: We provide data subject request APIs for Hosted and Dedicated; for Private you can implement them inside your network and use our delete endpoints to ensure caches are purged. We can demo the flow in the security deep dive.
[07:36] Robert: About analytics — does Redwood keep derived telemetry like embeddings or semantic hashes? Are those considered personal data?
[07:43] Priya: Embeddings and derived features are treated as telemetry. They can be considered personal data under certain regimes; we treat them as covered artifacts and can disable collection or ensure they are stored within required geo-boundaries.
[07:58] Jason: If we do a pilot, can we choose EU residency for the test account?
[08:01] Alex: Yes, we can stand up a pilot tenant in the EU region and configure logging to minimal retention and masking for sample tests.
[08:08] Maya: Ok, procurement will want to see contract language about breach notification timelines and subprocessor change notice periods.
[08:15] Alex: We can commit to 72-hour breach notification in our standard DPA and 30 days notice for subprocessor changes; negotiable for enterprise contracts.
[08:25] Robert: Also need details on MFA/SSO and RBAC mapping to our identity provider — SAML required.
[08:31] Priya: We support SAML SSO, SCIM for provisioning, and granular RBAC. For Private deployments you can map roles directly to your AD.
[08:41] Maya: Any gotchas around model caching and model shards — for example, does a model resident in EU ever reference tokens or weights hosted elsewhere?
[08:49] Priya: No, when we pin a model to a region we ensure model artifacts and weights are stored in-region; the runtime may fetch kernels but we don't stream user payloads outside the pinned region for Dedicated/Private. For Hosted there are certain managed services but we can provide documentation of data flows.
[09:07] Jason: Is there an option to run inference on-prem for the strictest flows?
[09:10] Alex: Yes — Redwood Private can be deployed on-premises; that gives you full control over data, keys, and network egress. That is the recommended path for regulated PII/PHI flows.
[09:20] Robert: For the security deep dive, we'll want a list of questions: key management details, consent and DSR audit, encryption algorithms, rotation policies, penetration test results, and how you handle zero-day incidents.
[09:31] Priya: We'll prepare a focused slide deck and an infra runbook. Also can include penetration test and purple team summary.
[09:39] Maya: Ok, sounds good. Quick recaps — we want: SOC2/ISO docs, subprocessor list, BYOK/HSM options, VPC/private architecture, pilot in EU, and pricing.
[09:52] Alex: Correct — I'll send the docs and Priya will share the architecture + pricing. Robert, can you coordinate the security deep dive scheduling?
[09:59] Robert: Yep, I'll propose times; aim for the week of Mar 15.
[10:03] Alex: Perfect. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with artifacts and calendar invites.

End of call.
